sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots increasingly function as an informal, de facto source of mental health support. This paper develops a governance framework for associated harms and specifies requirements for governance-ready design and evaluation.

sec.title: Method
sec.p: We conducted a purposive narrative review across seven databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar; searches through July 2026) using structured search query strings. Empirical evidence was systematically categorised and distinguished from theoretical psychoanalytic constructs. Findings informed a foundational design analysis of Eva, an unvalidated research case architecture informed by lived experience input.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We distinguish acute Type I harms (single-turn technical failures) from cumulative Type II harms (multi-session relational risks), characterised through digital psychological harm, the uncanny setting, relational hallucination, algorithmic collusion, AI-mediated psychosis, and epistemic exploitation. Governance-by-design responses include the SAFE-AI (i.e., Screening, Alignment, Facilitation, and Evaluation of AI-Enhanced Interventions) protocol, empathy by design, suitability screening, psychodynamic transcript analytics, bounded co-regulation, data sovereignty, and crisis-safe escalation rather than simulated therapy.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The central proposition of this paper is that generative AI may support mental health care only when bounded by governance-by-design, clinically informed safety mechanisms, and accountable human oversight, and only once these safeguards have been independently validated. Specifically, we identify three sets of conditions for governance-ready GenAI: clinical conditions, including suitability screening and crisis-safe escalation; relational conditions, including bounded roles, anti-collusive friction, and longitudinal monitoring of Type II drift; and operational conditions, including human oversight, data sovereignty, auditability, and independent validation.

abstract.title: KEY POINTS
abstract.p: What is already known about this topic:

(1) AI as an Unregulated Adjunct: GenAI chatbots have quietly become an informal, de facto source of mental health support, with individuals increasingly relying on them as accessible psychoeducation and support, often outside of formal clinical oversight.

(2) Significant clinical and relational risks: Rapid adoption exposes vulnerable clients to inadequate crisis responses, reinforcement of harmful ideation or beliefs, intensified distress and emotional dysregulation, privacy risks, emotional dependency, and epistemic exploitation.

(3) The clinical governance gap: Mental health AI has outpaced clinical evidence and safety oversight, leaving practitioners without consistent, trauma-informed frameworks for evaluating, monitoring, or integrating clients’ use of these tools.

(1) A clinical harm typology: This paper distinguishes acute technical failures (Type I harms) from cumulative relational risks (Type II harms), introducing constructs such as algorithmic collusion and relational hallucination to help clinicians understand long-term human-AI interaction risks.

(2) Trauma-Informed Governance-by-Design: Eva is presented as a provisional Augmented Emotional Intelligence (AEI) case architecture informed by people with lived experience of neurodivergence (ADHD) and trauma. Its gradual adaptation model respects individual processing preferences and avoids the forced neurotypical pacing or engagement-optimised attachment in some commercial systems, particularly consumer AI companions.

(3) A Collaborative Clinical Workflow: The framework provides a practical roadmap for psychological practices, advocating for the integration of digital navigators in a collaborative care triad, and proposing the use of psychodynamic transcript analytics to monitor a client’s autonomy, dependency, and transition to specialist human care.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Post-COVID-19 digital transformation has accelerated AI chatbots as scalable, low-barrier mental health supports, while exposing critical clinical risks like emotional dependence and inadequate crisis response (Balcombe, 2026), as well as the phenomenon of “Seemingly Conscious AI”, where anthropomorphic user perceptions introduce severe ethical and behavioural hazards (Bariach et al., 2026).

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) platforms are rapidly entering mental health research, education, care delivery, and everyday help seeking. However, it is essential to distinguish general-purpose commercial models such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, which operate in a regulatory blind spot, from clinically oriented architectures such as the Wysa Digital Referral Assistant, which prioritise safety through structured clinical boundaries (Asman et al., 2025; Balcombe, 2023, 2026; Han & Zhao, 2026; Heinz et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025; Ni & Jia, 2025).

In this paper, “governance-ready” refers specifically to architectural and structural readiness to undergo systematic safety evaluation, auditability, and risk mitigation, rather than a claim of demonstrated clinical efficacy or empirical safety. An Australian Handbook for Responsible AI in Mental Health Support (Krome & Guy, 2026) illustrates this orientation through a 13-question framework for deploying digital mental health tools as safety-critical complements to care, covering safeguards such as named clinical veto authority, sovereign data storage, demographic equity auditing, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.

General-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) serve many tasks. Some commercial systems, particularly consumer AI companions, are optimised for engagement, retention, and immediate satisfaction rather than clinical safety (Refoua et al., 2026). AI companions offer accessible, low-cost, continuously available support for psychoeducation and reflection, particularly where wait times, stigma, geography, finances, loneliness, trauma, or neurodivergent communication needs constrain access. However, commercial systems are generally neither designed nor validated as mental health interventions and may lack transparent data practices, crisis pathways, suitability screening, cultural adaptation, human oversight, and efficacy testing (Balcombe, 2026; Bodner et al., 2026; Connolly & Torous, 2026; Nakagomi et al., 2026; Olisaeloka et al., 2026). Reviews also identify uneven evidence, safety mechanisms, governance, and knowledge of long-term effects (Abd-Alrazaq et al., 2019, 2020; Gaffney et al., 2019; Khosravi & Izadi, 2026; Rahsepar Meadi et al., 2025; Vaidyam et al., 2019; Wajid et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2024). Suitability screening therefore assesses whether AI support fits a user’s profile and goals or whether human care is required.

AI-mediated mental health support is no longer marginal. A nationally representative survey of US adolescents and young adults reported that 19.2% had used commercial AI chatbots for mental health advice, up from 13.1% the previous year (McBain et al., 2026). Refoua et al. (2026) similarly argue that general purpose LLMs have become de facto mental health resources because of accessibility, anonymity, low cost, and gaps in formal care. Nelson et al. (2026) add that the safety debate must move beyond whether systems are general purpose or specialised and instead ask what they have been trained to do, for whom, over what time horizon, and with what harms.

Behavioural science, clinical psychology, human-computer interaction (HCI), and safety engineering measure symptoms, usability, observable behaviour, technical failures, and predefined safety events. Psychodynamic constructs are used here as a complementary lens for generating testable hypotheses about longitudinal changes in the relational meaning of AI use, including agency attribution, expectations of containment, responses to limits, reflective distance, and movement towards or away from human care.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Recently, Linardon et al. (2026) issued a multidisciplinary call to action, warning that the rapid proliferation of mental health AI has outpaced clinical evidence, safety oversight, and equitable governance. This narrative review, critical perspective and foundational design analysis respond to that call by proposing a governance framework anchored by Augmented Emotional Intelligence (AEI) (Balcombe, 2026) and the SAFE-AI (i.e., Screening, Alignment, Facilitation, and Evaluation of AI-Enhanced Interventions) protocol (Haber et al., 2025). By introducing Eva as a governance-by-design case architecture, this paper illustrates how bounded memory, human-in-the-loop oversight, and crisis-safe pathways can mitigate both acute technical failures and cumulative psychological harms.

While early deployments highlight the potential of conversational AI, the rapid proliferation of these tools introduces significant clinical risks prior to formal intervention, including harmful ideation, reinforcement of distorted beliefs, intensification of psychological distress, and severe emotional dysregulation (Morrin et al., 2026; Olisaeloka et al., 2026). Consequently, this paper is guided by one central research question: What clinical, relational, and operational conditions must governance-ready GenAI satisfy to provide bounded mental health support without increasing psychological or relational harm?

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This paper combines a purposive narrative review and critical perspective across clinical, community, and population levels with Eva, a foundational research case for bounded memory, consent, trauma-responsive behaviour, privacy, auditability, human oversight, and safe human–AI co-regulation. It examines support for emotion regulation, psychoeducation, stepped care, crisis escalation, clinician oversight, and transition to human care without diagnostic or therapeutic claims, while considering access, stigma, neurodivergence, trauma, digital literacy, governance, policy, and equity. Consistent with the definition given in the Introduction, Eva is examined for its readiness to undergo governance evaluation, not for demonstrated safety or clinical effectiveness.

sec.title: Design and evidence sources
sec.p: The paper drew on peer-reviewed research on AI in mental health as well as two foundational psychoanalytic sources on containment and alpha-function (Bion, 1962, 1965). Sources were found through database and targeted online searches, including PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Search terms combined concepts such as (“AI chatbot” OR “generative AI chatbot” OR “general purpose chatbot” OR “commercial chatbot” OR “AI companion” OR “AI therapist” OR “conversational agent” OR “large language model”) AND (“mental health” OR “digital mental health”) AND (“AI safety” OR “AI governance”). Searches prioritised literature from 2018 to 8 July 2026 (date conducted), while earlier foundational sources were included where conceptually necessary. The narrative review process followed guidance on narrative reviews and behavioural intervention research, including multi-source searching, keyword identification from relevant articles, abstract and full-text review, and thematic synthesis (Demiris et al., 2019; Green et al., 2006).

A strict systematic review or meta-analysis was not conducted because the field is novel, highly interdisciplinary, and rapidly evolving, and because our objective is conceptual framework synthesis rather than effect size estimation. The review therefore sought to critically synthesise evidence across heterogeneous clinical, relational, ethical, safety, accuracy, and governance domains that could not readily be reduced to a common effect estimate. Literature was purposively identified to address domains considered theoretically and clinically relevant to the proposed framework, while allowing additional concerns to emerge inductively during the review process.

sec.title: Selection and synthesis
sec.p: Screening of abstracts and titles and full text where applicable was conducted by the first author (LB). Where empirical findings conflicted, greater weight was given to controlled and systematic evidence, and discrepancies are reported rather than reconciled. No formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment was undertaken, consistent with the conceptual aim of the review; instead, evidentiary weight was differentiated by study design.
To maintain evidentiary clarity and avoid overstating theoretical claims, retrieved literature was categorised during data extraction into two categories:

Category A, Empirical Clinical Evidence: Comprising randomised controlled trials, scoping reviews, systematic reviews, and observational user experience studies assessing chatbot effectiveness, safety benchmarks, or clinical outcomes (e.g., Abd-Alrazaq et al., 2020; Heinz et al., 2025; Nelson et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Empirical evidence was weighted to establish baseline technical safety, accuracy, and clinical efficacy.

Category B, Theoretical and Psychoanalytic Frameworks: Comprising conceptual papers, bi-logical semiotic analyses, and psychoanalytic theories of containment (e.g., Andrisano Ruggieri et al., 2025; Bion, 1962; Holohan & Fiske, 2021). Theoretical literature was utilised specifically to interpret cumulative relational, symbolic, and epistemic risks unfolding over extended usage horizons.

Sources were included if they addressed AI systems used for mental health, emotional support, psychological wellbeing, screening, monitoring, education, care delivery, ethical or policy issues, safety, effectiveness, user experience, crisis handling, bias, privacy, human oversight, or implementation science outcomes. Sources were excluded if they focused solely on non-digital interventions, physical rehabilitation robotics without psychological relevance, commercial marketing material without substantive framework contribution, or lacked full-text access. Sources reporting null or adverse findings were retained to limit confirmation bias.

Sources were mapped to AI use, safety, effectiveness, governance, human–AI interaction, underserved populations, implementation, and policy. Recurring themes (access, personalisation, crisis handling, bias, privacy, digital psychological harm, synthetic attachment harm, epistemic instability, and human oversight) were integrated with the Eva design case to develop the AEI framework.

sec.title: Governance synthesis
sec.p: AI mental health systems span screening, psychoeducation, navigation, conversational support, clinician augmentation, education, and digital interventions. They may improve detection, personalisation, efficiency, and low-intensity support, but evidence quality, adherence, validation, and long-term safety remain uneven (Feng et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Mayor, 2025; Volpato et al., 2025). Mental health also involves vulnerability, crisis, culture, sensitive data, and relational meaning; conversational fluency does not prevent fabrication, over-mirroring, simulated intimacy, distorted uncertainty, or displacement of human care (Balcombe, 2026; Holohan & Fiske, 2021; Khawaja & Bélisle-Pipon, 2023; Xie et al., 2023). Users may value an “emotional sanctuary”, yet generic warnings or abrupt clinical redirection can be experienced as rejection, supporting trauma-informed escalation that preserves continuity while moving users towards human care (Siddals et al., 2024).

Evaluations of the Wysa and PATH (i.e., Personalised Artificial Intelligence Therapy) apps similarly found that users valued immediate, non-judgemental support but reported repetitive responses and technical glitches, reinforcing the need to balance emotional continuity with crisis-safe responses (Chaudhry & Debi, 2024; Powell et al., 2026).

The governance gap is both technical and relational. Timmons et al. (2022) called for assessing and mitigating bias in AI applications for mental health. SAFE-AI was subsequently developed by Haber et al. (2025) as a structured framework for clinicians introducing GenAI to patients, and Refoua et al. (2026) recommended it for addressing misinformation, hallucination, privacy risk, bias, emotional dependency, and erosion of autonomy.

sec.title: Clinical harm typology
sec.p:
Nelson et al. (2026) distinguish Type I harms, acute technical failures occurring within a single prompt or brief exchange (such as unsafe crisis responses, factual hallucinations, or emotional volatility), from Type II harms, which are cumulative risks that unfold across prolonged, multi-session interactions (such as sycophancy, dependency, and delusional reinforcement). While Type I harms can be evaluated through automated benchmarks and single-prompt red-teaming, Type II harms emerge gradually through sustained interaction. Building on this distinction, we propose that synthetic attachment harm, algorithmic collusion (Andrisano Ruggieri et al., 2026), and epistemic exploitation (Refoua et al., 2026), serve as specific relational mechanisms through which Type II harms develop. A single sycophantic response is therefore a Type I event, whereas a repeated pattern of sycophantic validation across sessions constitutes a Type II harm; Figure 1 illustrates this consolidation. To further elaborate, a single response that supplies unsafe information to a user disclosing suicidal intent is a Type I harm: it is identifiable within one exchange, detectable through benchmark testing, and addressed by correcting the system. By contrast, Type II harm is visible only across sessions. For example, a user who consults a chatbot over weeks before every decision, describes it as the only one who understands, and postpones contact with their clinician, may experience no single harmful exchange. Type I harms therefore call for incident reporting and technical correction, whereas Type II harms call for clinical inquiry into the client’s pattern of AI use, longitudinal monitoring, and where indicated, a supported transition to human care. In addition, synthetic attachment harm describes the relational, emotional, and epistemic harms that occur when users form attachment bonds with AI systems that simulate reciprocity and care, leading to emotional dependence, relational displacement, and impaired reality testing.

Figure 1 presents a longitudinal harm-escalation model for Type II harms that may not be detected in routine practice or captured by static benchmarks. These risks therefore require extended evaluation across sessions using established behavioural and clinical measures alongside the provisional relational indicators proposed in this paper, such as increasing dependency, loss of reflective distance, resistance to relational limits, and delayed transition to human care. The psychodynamic and psychological constructs are conceptual hypotheses rather than established diagnoses or validated measures; their added value must be tested through operational definitions, independent coding, inter-rater reliability, and comparison with existing HCI, dependency, anthropomorphism, and clinical outcome measures.

sec.title: Provisional research constructs and construct hierarchy
sec.p: This paper proposes a set of provisional research constructs for understanding AI-related mental health risk: digital psychological harm, the uncanny setting, relational hallucination, algorithmic collusion, AI-mediated psychosis, and epistemic exploitation. These are not diagnostic categories; instead, they describe how emotionally fluent AI systems may destabilise users when conversational responsiveness is mistaken for reliable support.

Digital psychological harm refers to a continuum of emotional distress arising from destabilising AI interactions, including worry, anxiety, low mood, shame, dependency, excessive reassurance seeking, cognitive offloading, and traumatic distress. Four pathways are especially relevant: 1) algorithmic harm from inconsistent, unsafe, or hallucinated outputs; 2) synthetic attachment harm from emotionally significant bonds with systems that simulate care; 3) epistemic harm from disrupted trust in perception or reality boundaries; and 4) cognitive overload harm from high-volume AI-mediated emotional processing. These pathways may interact over time, making long-term evaluation essential (Nelson et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025).

The psychodynamic notion of the uncanny setting clarifies why these risks are not merely technical. Therapeutic dialogue depends on symbolic containment, boundaries, silence, interpretation, and the clinician’s capacity to receive and transform affect. Andrisano Ruggieri et al. (2025) argue that therapeutic chatbots may create a pseudo-therapeutic space in which simulated responsiveness appears relational while lacking transference work, countertransference, and symbolic transformation. This argument builds on psychoanalytic and semiotic work on algorithmic mediation, the digital unconscious, anthropomorphic attribution, and the limits of machine-generated signs (Hamamra & Uebel, 2025; Picca, 2025; Siporin, 2025). In Bion’s terms, the system may return emotionally charged material without alpha-function containment (Bion, 1962, 1965; Holohan & Fiske, 2021).

When users in acute distress interact with LLMs, the resulting harm is often ontological rather than merely technical (Andrisano Ruggieri et al., 2026). Drawing on bi-logical theory, these systems have a semiotic deficit: they master the formal asymmetry of language without the emotional, embodied “symmetric base” needed for authentic care. In heightened vulnerability, such as suicidal crisis, this dynamic can trigger a “relational hallucination”, in which the user invests the AI with real relational qualities. Designed to gratify literal requests rather than address latent emotional demands, commercial chatbots risk complying with harmful intentions. This “algorithmic collusion” amplifies destructive trajectories rather than safely redirecting them: the system ratifies the manifest demand while leaving the latent one untouched, agreeing where a clinician would inquire and confirming a destabilising trajectory rather than interrupting it.

AI-mediated psychosis is proposed by Andrisano Ruggieri et al. (2026) as a relational and epistemic destabilisation process, not as a claim that AI biologically causes psychosis (Morrin et al., 2026; Olisaeloka et al., 2026). It describes situations in which synthetic agency attribution, delusional reinforcement, identity diffusion, derealisation, or symbolic collapse is triggered in the user or is intensified through prolonged AI interaction. Risk may be higher when loneliness, trauma, neurodivergence, cognitive impairment (e.g., dementia), dissociation, prior psychosis, unmet attachment needs, or social isolation intersect with emotionally immersive AI use (Balcombe, 2026; Khosravi & Izadi, 2026; McBain et al., 2026). This destabilisation is compounded by what Refoua et al. (2026) term “epistemic exploitation”. Because conversational AI lacks genuine intentionality, bodily attunement, and moral agency, it offers only a simulated “pseudo-empathy”. When highly vulnerable users develop misplaced epistemic trust in these non-sentient systems, they risk outsourcing their emotional processing. Over time, this transactional exchange can erode user autonomy, causing individuals to gradually lose confidence in their own critical thinking and internal capacity for self-reflection.

Taken together, the constructs form one provisional explanatory sequence. On the system side, a semiotic deficit, formal fluency without a symmetric affective base, means that emotionally charged material is returned without alpha-function containment; when the system also ratifies the manifest demand, this becomes algorithmic collusion. On the user side, heightened vulnerability favours relational hallucination, the investment of the system with relational qualities it lacks. The encounter of the two constitutes the uncanny setting; repeated over time, it may lead to epistemic exploitation and, in vulnerable users, to Type II outcomes described here as digital psychological harm or AI-mediated psychosis. sec.title: Operationalising psychodynamic transcript analytics
sec.p: The proposed psychodynamic terms add relational interpretation rather than rename established measures. Anthropomorphism concerns attributing human characteristics to a system; projection concerns user-derived meanings, intentions, or affective qualities that organise subsequent interaction. Dependency measures assess reliance, distress on separation, or displacement of other supports, whereas attachment escalation describes increasing emotional significance, exclusivity, or authority across sessions. Symbolic failure provisionally denotes difficulty retaining the system as a representational tool rather than an intentional relational other, indicated by claims that it uniquely knows, chooses, loves, persecutes, or communicates with the user, resistance to reminders of its non-human status, or treatment of its outputs as privileged evidence about reality. These distinctions require discriminant validation against existing anthropomorphism, dependency, therapeutic-alliance, and qualitative HCI measures.

Psychodynamic transcript analytics is proposed as a provisional, theory-informed qualitative coding framework. Its purpose is to supplement ordinary thematic or content analysis by coding what topics occur, how the user positions the system relationally across time as well as how the interaction changes after uncertainty, disagreement, boundary reminders, or referral to human care.

A future codebook would specify inclusion and exclusion criteria for four candidate domains: agency attribution and projection; expectations of symbolic containment; sycophantic collusion and loss of reflective distance; and symbolic failure or reality-boundary erosion. Two independent raters would code predefined transcript units as present, absent, or indeterminate before resolving disagreements. Reliability would be reported for each domain using Cohen’s kappa or a prevalence-appropriate alternative, with confidence intervals, disagreement examples, and tests of convergent and discriminant validity. Because no codebook or reliability estimate currently exists, the framework remains a research proposal rather than a validated method for identifying Type II relational harms.

sec.title: Eva as a case architecture and governance design
sec.p: Clinically, the most immediate relational risks are harmful ideation, reinforcement of distorted or harmful beliefs, intensification of distress, and emotional dysregulation. In Bion’s (1962) terms, these involve raw, unmetabolised affect that the user cannot yet think about. A human container receives such material and returns it in a form that can be thought; a conversational system cannot perform this alpha-function, but it can simulate its surface, returning the material fluently yet untransformed, or validated rather than contained. Eva’s safeguards are therefore not proposed as a substitute container. Reflective friction and uncertainty signalling are intended to avoid ratifying harmful ideation; trauma-responsive pacing is intended to reduce load on an already dysregulated user; and crisis-safe escalation is intended to route uncontained affect towards a human capable of containment.

The AEI framework (Balcombe, 2026) integrates real-time emotional adaptation with ethical boundaries around agency, privacy, and consent. AEI systems do not claim to feel, care, diagnose, or provide therapy. By being firmly constrained by clinical safeguards, AEI systems offer tools for emotional clarity, grounding, journalling, music listening and psychoeducation. To further empower users and maintain strict boundaries, these systems also integrate pacing controls, bounded memory, uncertainty signalling, and trauma responsive runtime behaviour. Furthermore, these systems are designed to trigger clear crisis support escalation to local emergency resources and helplines, thereby helping the necessary movement towards human support.

Eva is a provisional AEI case architecture informed by lived experience and multicultural input, including users with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), as well as trauma-informed and Indigenous Australian perspectives. These were gathered through iterative informal feedback over more than one year; this consultation was not conducted as a formal research study. Iterative feedback addressed conversational pacing, sensory-processing preferences, and avoidance of forced neurotypical interaction styles. Its proposed capabilities are design hypotheses rather than evidence of clinical efficacy.

Eva combines transparent role limits, user-controlled pacing, structured consent, and separate opt-in long-term memory. Routine conversations are not retained in long-term memory, and personal context requires explicit consent. Its trauma-responsive runtime behaviour is designed to detect distress and adjust responses in real time, with the intention of reducing cognitive overload, without making clinical claims or attempting to diagnose the user. Where high-risk content is detected, Eva is designed to provide immediate crisis resources and facilitate connection to local human services, while maintaining supportive continuity. However, these functions are design hypotheses requiring empirical validation.

Table A1 (see Appendix A) links Eva’s bounded architecture to intended purposes, mitigated risks, implementation and evidence status, and validation requirements. It distinguishes single-exchange delusion support from cumulative delusional reinforcement and treats synthetic attachment harm as an AI-dependent bond that displaces human relationships.

SAFE-AI provides a practical governance cycle for systems such as Eva. Screening determines whether AI-mediated support is appropriate and identifies users who need human care. Alignment configures role boundaries, emotional intensity, crisis pathways, communication preferences, privacy settings, and oversight. Facilitation provides bounded co-regulation, psychoeducation, grounding, and transition-to-care support. Evaluation monitors safety, effectiveness, equity, dependency risk, implementation outcomes, and Type I and Type II harms.

Table B1 (see Appendix B) translates the SAFE-AI cycle into Eva-specific governance safeguards, showing how each stage addresses clinical and relational risks through measurable evaluation indicators.

Data sovereignty, distinct from technical data security and retention, concerns the collective right of communities to govern data about them. Eva’s design draws on the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance (Carroll et al., 2020) and the Maiam nayri Wingara principles in the Australian context (Maiam nayri Wingara Indigenous Data Sovereignty Collective & Australian Indigenous Governance Institute, 2018), alongside Ownership, Control, Access, and Possession (OCAP) principles developed for First Nations, Canada (First Nations Information Governance Centre, n.d.). Engagement, Governance, Access, and Protection (EGAP) principles, developed for health data concerning Black communities in Canada (Black Health Equity Working Group, 2021), inform community accountability. Separately, Eva is intended to operationalise “empathy by design” (Howcroft & Blake, 2025) by using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to maintain structured long-term memory separation without continuous model retraining.

We distinguish privacy, security, retention and deletion, access control, model training boundaries (not intended to be applied to Eva’s data, as RAG processes context in-memory rather than updating the AI model’s internal weights), and third-party processing; data sovereignty is to be managed separately as a collective right.

Eva’s gradual adaptation model respects individual neurodivergent communication preferences without treating neurodivergent users as a homogeneous group. It avoids forced neurotypical conversational pacing, allows user-controlled interaction depth, and uses visual glyphs for explicit memory opt-in. Overall, Eva illustrates a framework for AI in mental health governance and collaborative care triad architecture (see Figure 2) through user interaction, harms identification, safeguard and mental health care implementation, as well as ongoing evaluation and audits. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In answer to the guiding question, the synthesis identifies three sets of conditions that governance-ready GenAI must satisfy: clinical conditions, including suitability screening and crisis-safe escalation; relational conditions, including bounded roles, anti-collusive friction, and longitudinal monitoring of Type II drift; and operational conditions, including accountable human oversight, data sovereignty, auditability, and independent validation.

The central proposition of this paper is that generative AI may support mental health care only when bounded by governance-by-design, clinically informed safety mechanisms, and accountable human oversight, and only once these safeguards have been independently validated.

The contribution of this paper is the integration of theory and practice for advancing governance of AI in mental health. The Type I/Type II distinction (Nelson et al., 2026), SAFE-AI, and NASSS are adopted from existing work. The novelty is the specific way these are linked: psychodynamic constructs are used to specify the mechanisms through which Type II harms may develop. In addition, each mechanism is tied to a governance safeguard and a proposed validation method (Table 1). Lastly, Eva is used to show how these requirements could be translated into architecture and evaluated.

sec.title: Limitations, reflexivity, and future validation
sec.p: This conceptual synthesis proposes a foundation for empirical work. Author positioning is relevant: the team includes psychiatry, clinical psychology, applied psychology/informatics, AI-industry, founder, and doctoral research experience. This breadth supports integration of trauma-informed care with research on AI-mediated psychosis, epistemic instability, and digital attachment, but also requires explicit reflexivity.

The lead author’s dual role of researcher/founder introduces potential interpretive or confirmation bias regarding the perceived feasibility and safety of Eva’s architecture. To mitigate this bias, Eva is presented strictly as an unvalidated conceptual testbed and hypothesis-generating design case rather than evidence of effectiveness, underscoring the need for future independent, third-party empirical validation.

The purposive narrative synthesis is not exhaustive, and screening by a single author may have introduced selection bias. In addition, the evidence base is heterogeneous: claims about Type I harms and user experience rest largely on empirical sources, whereas the proposed mechanisms of Type II harm rest mainly on conceptual and theoretical sources and should be read as hypotheses.

Psychodynamic transcript analytics has not been converted into a validated codebook, tested for inter-rater reliability, or shown to add value beyond established HCI, clinical, behavioural, dependency, anthropomorphism, or qualitative measures. Rapid technical, regulatory, and evidentiary change may also require revision of the manuscript’s implementation and policy claims. While provisional, the psychodynamic constructs are designed to capture what behavioural measures cannot see by construction, namely the relational meaning the user attributes to the system over time.

Future validation should therefore prioritise independent evaluation, participatory design with users and practitioners, diverse beta testing, longitudinal safety assessment, and real-world implementation studies. Evaluation should also include users who did not participate in the system’s original design, because systems informed by lived experience may appear safer or more intuitive to their founding users than to broader populations. These studies should examine whether AEI systems preserve autonomy, reduce dependency, support crisis-safe pathways, and improve transition to human care.

sec.title: Implications for research, practice, policy, and future evaluation
sec.p: The framework has implications across five overlapping domains. First, research should move beyond short interaction tests and symptom-only outcomes to include longitudinal transcript analysis, dependency and attachment indicators, escalation failures, equity outcomes, user autonomy, and movement towards human care. Type I harms can be assessed through crisis-response benchmarks, but Type II harms require extended, multi-session evaluation capable of detecting slow relational and epistemic drift.

Second, clinical practice should without judgement routinely assess clients’ chatbot use to uncover unmet needs, loneliness, or trauma exposure. For trauma-affected users, AI engagement is recommended to follow the TRUST (i.e., Trauma-informed, Responsible development, User-centric multidisciplinary input, Safety and effectiveness, Treatment equity) framework (Ridings et al., 2026). Digital navigators can help integrate these tools into clinical workflows (Gorban et al., 2024; Strudwick et al., 2025; Torous et al., 2025), functioning best within a collaborative care triad where clinicians actively endorse the technology and engage in shared decision-making. This adjunctive approach is reinforced by empirical evidence: users of one AI-enabled intervention described GenAI primarily as a between-session assistive tool for symptom tracking and coping to complement face-to-face human therapy (Powell et al., 2026).

Third, policy should distinguish general-purpose LLMs used for mental health from systems intentionally designed for mental health support. Both require governance. However, specialised systems should become governance-ready by meeting higher standards for transparency, crisis safety, privacy, suitability screening, human oversight, auditability, cultural relevance, and independent evaluation. Regulation should examine what the system does, what claims are made, what data are processed, what risks are foreseeable, and what safeguards are demonstrably effective, rather than relying on whether a product is marketed as specialised (Nelson et al., 2026; Refoua et al., 2026; Shim, 2026).

Fourth, education for mental health clinicians, students, users, developers, and organisations should include AI literacy, digital mental health literacy, limitations of chatbot advice, privacy and data governance, crisis boundaries, bias and cultural safety, and the relational risks of anthropomorphic design. Education should also emphasise that safe AI support is not achieved through empathy simulation, but through bounded roles, transparent uncertainty, escalation pathways, and accountable human systems. For Eva, these implications translate into a research programme rather than a product claim. Evaluation should be staged, independent, and comparative, moving from usability and acceptability testing to beta evaluation with diverse users, clinician and digital navigator workflow studies, and longer-term monitoring of benefits, harms, and transition-to-care outcomes. The evaluation protocols within the Assessment Framework for Mental Health Apps (Mental Health Commission of Canada, 2023) are a useful guide.

Fifth, to make future empirical evaluation methodologically actionable, research on case architectures like Eva must categorise outcomes across three distinct categories:
Primary Safety Outcomes: Acute crisis detection accuracy, rate of Type I single turn response failures, jailbreak vulnerability, and crisis escalation reliability.
Secondary Clinical and Relational Outcomes: Longitudinal Type II harm indicators, including changes in user autonomy, dependency markers, emotional dysregulation, and transition to human care.
Implementation Outcomes: Evaluated via the NASSS framework (Shin et al., 2025), including feasibility, acceptability, digital navigator workflow integration, cost, and equity across diverse populations.

Validation should use mixed methods and the NASSS framework to compare bounded AEI architectures with publicly available LLMs across clinical, organisational, and user contexts. A staged programme should progress from de-identified transcript analysis and simulation-based safety testing to supervised beta studies, implementation pilots, and comparative evaluations. Outcomes should include emotional regulation, autonomy, dependency risk, crisis-pathway activation, help-seeking, transition to care, privacy comprehension, clinician acceptability, digital navigator workload, cost, equity, and cultural fit.

As general-purpose LLMs expand multimodal capabilities, evaluation must distinguish recognition of observable affect from inference of emotion, clinical state, or suicide risk. Although models can match or exceed human benchmarks for static facial-emotion recognition (Nelson et al., 2025), inferring crisis directly from facial or acoustic signals risks epistemic overreach, surveillance, and bias. Future research should therefore test whether visual and auditory inputs improve crisis detection without producing inappropriate intervention.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This paper proposes a framework for making GenAI in mental health governance-ready and is organised around three sets of conditions: clinical (suitability screening, crisis-safe escalation), relational (bounded roles, anti-collusive friction, tracking of Type II drift), and operational (human oversight, data sovereignty, auditability, independent validation).

The proposed typology distinguishes acute technical failures from cumulative relational risks and explains why conversational fluency cannot substitute for the symbolic containment, accountability, and relational basis of human therapy. Eva illustrates an unvalidated governance-by-design architecture using bounded memory, crisis pathways, data-sovereignty safeguards, and accountable human oversight.

Ultimately, navigating this landscape requires moving beyond superficial conversational fluency toward robust, independently validated frameworks, as generative AI may safely support mental health care only when bounded by governance-by-design, clinically informed safety mechanisms, and accountable human oversight that firmly secure it as an ethical complement to human-led care.

sec.p: Claude and Co-pilot were used for enhancing idea generation and exploration, as well as proofreading and grammar checking. AI-generated material was verified and appropriately modified to reflect the authors’ research and style of writing.

sec.p: No datasets were generated or analysed for this manuscript.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: This article does not report research involving human participants. Lived experience and multicultural feedback informing Eva’s design was gathered informally and was not conducted as a research study; ethics approval was therefore not sought.
